MNR moved from MD slot 2 to slot 18 (has starting popularity, fits revolutionary nationalism). Slot 7 = the left-nationalist officers around Juan José Torres. Slot 20 = Military-Peasant Pact. 0.name: Movimiento Popular Cristiano
0.text:
The Christian Popular Movement was created in 1965 as the political vehicle of General René Barrientos Ortuño, who ruled Bolivia until his death in a helicopter crash in April 1969. Without its caudillo the movement is leaderless, and Ovando's coup of September 1969 has pushed his followers out of power.

Barrientismo stands for anti-communism, close alignment with the United States, generous terms for foreign investors and a firm hand against the miners' unions. Its supporters are conservative officers such as Colonel Hugo Banzer Suárez, Cochabamba notables and politicians who fear Ovando's turn to nationalization. Its leverage lies in the barracks and in Washington's goodwill.

1.name: Partido Demócrata Cristiano
1.text:
The Christian Democratic Party grew out of the Social Christian Party founded in 1954 and adopted its present name in the 1960s. Led by Benjamín Miguel Harb and Remo Di Natale, it took part in the Barrientos coalition and now watches the military government from the sidelines.

The party draws on Catholic social teaching: social justice, cooperatives, education and representative democracy, opposed both to Marxism and to the old oligarchy. It is friendly to the West and to Christian Democrats in Chile and Venezuela. Its base is small, mostly urban professionals and Catholic students, but it enjoys the sympathy of parts of the Church.

2.name: Partido Revolucionario Auténtico
2.text:
The Authentic Revolutionary Party was founded in 1960 by Wálter Guevara Arze, one of the leaders of the 1952 revolution, after he broke with Víctor Paz Estenssoro over the presidential succession. It served in the Barrientos government and has lost its posts under Ovando.

The party claims the moderate heritage of the national revolution: land reform and nationalized mines, but also constitutional government, fiscal discipline and good relations with the United States. It rejects both the left of the unions and military rule without end. Its base is a circle of middle-class politicians and lawyers in La Paz and Cochabamba.

3.name: Partido Revolucionario de la Izquierda Nacional
3.english: Revolutionary Party of the Nationalist Left
3.native_full: Partido Revolucionario de la Izquierda Nacional
3.text:
The Revolutionary Party of the Nationalist Left was founded in 1964 by Juan Lechín Oquendo, the legendary leader of the miners' federation and the Bolivian Workers' Center, after his break with Paz Estenssoro. Persecuted under Barrientos, Lechín is again active as Ovando relaxes repression.

The party embodies the labour wing of the 1952 revolution: workers' co-government in the mines, wage rises, union autonomy and nationalization of foreign oil. It is anti-imperialist but not communist. Its leverage lies in the mining camps of Siglo XX and Catavi and in Lechín's ability to call general strikes.
3.wiki: Revolutionary Party of the Nationalist Left

4.name: Partido Comunista de Bolivia
4.text:
The Communist Party of Bolivia was founded in 1950 and follows the Moscow line. Damaged by its ambiguous role during Che Guevara's 1967 guerrilla, when Mario Monje refused support, it is now led by first secretary Jorge Kolle Cueto and works openly again under Ovando.

The party seeks an anti-imperialist front of workers, peasants and patriotic officers rather than armed struggle. It welcomes the nationalization of Gulf Oil and the opening of relations with the Soviet Union. Its strength lies among miners, teachers and university students, and in its links to the Soviet embassy opened in La Paz.

5.name: Ejército de Liberación Nacional
5.text:
The National Liberation Army is the guerrilla organization founded by Ernesto 'Che' Guevara in 1967. After Che's death, Guido 'Inti' Peredo rebuilt it, but he was killed by police in La Paz in September 1969. His brother Osvaldo 'Chato' Peredo now prepares a new rural front, recruiting students.

The ELN rejects elections and military reformism alike and holds that only armed struggle can free Bolivia and the continent from imperialism. It draws on Cuban support, radical students and Christian youth. Its numbers are small, but its martyrs make it a powerful symbol across Latin America.

6.name: Falange Socialista Boliviana
6.text:
The Bolivian Socialist Falange was founded in Chile in 1937 by Óscar Únzaga de la Vega on the model of the Spanish Falange. Long the main opposition to the MNR, it lost its founder in 1959 and is now led by Mario Gutiérrez Gutiérrez.

The Falange preaches Catholic nationalism, hierarchy, corporatism and fierce anti-communism, while mistrusting foreign capital and the liberal West. It bitterly opposes Ovando's opening to the left. Its strength lies in Santa Cruz, among students and the urban middle classes, and among officers who share its hostility to the unions.

7.name: Militares Nacionalistas
7.text:
The Nationalist Officers are the left-leaning faction of the high command gathered around General Juan José Torres, commander-in-chief of the armed forces and one of the architects of the September 1969 coup. They inspired the 'Revolutionary Mandate of the Armed Forces' and the seizure of Gulf Oil.

The faction wants a national revolution led by the army in alliance with workers and peasants, state control of oil and minerals, and distance from Washington, taking Peru's Velasco as a model. Its leverage lies in key commands and in its growing understanding with the miners' unions and the students.

8.name: Círculo del Imam Musa
8.text:
The Circle of Imam Musa is a handful of Lebanese Shia traders in La Paz and Santa Cruz who follow the work of Imam Musa al-Sadr, head since 1969 of the Supreme Islamic Shia Council in Beirut. They gather in private homes and keep a low profile.

They seek dignity and representation for the Shia of south Lebanon and send money home to their villages. In Bolivia they avoid politics, staying loyal to whoever governs and wary of both blocs. Their only leverage is commerce and family networks reaching from the Andes to Lebanon.

9.name: Fieles del Ayatolá
9.text:
The Faithful of the Ayatollah are a tiny group of Shia immigrants who circulate the sermons of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled in Najaf, where he has just expounded government by the Islamic jurist. They have no premises and no legal standing in Bolivia.

They reject monarchy and secular nationalism and condemn both Washington and Moscow. Their horizon is a revolution in Iran rather than in Bolivia. Politically they are invisible, but their conviction and contacts with the wider Shia world make them the seed of a militant network.

10.name: Los Peregrinos de La Meca
10.text:
The Pilgrims of Mecca are a small group of Muslim merchants of Arab and South Asian origin who receive literature and occasional donations from the Muslim World League, founded in Mecca in 1962. They pray together in rented rooms in La Paz and dream of a mosque.

They teach quietist Islam approved by Riyadh: obedience to rulers, distance from politics and firm anti-communism. They look warily at Ovando's courtship of the Soviet Union but stay silent. Their leverage is Gulf money and the respectability of trading families in the capital.

11.name: Célula del Califato
11.text:
The Caliphate Cell is a few Arab students in La Paz who have come across the pamphlets of Hizb ut-Tahrir, Taqiuddin al-Nabhani's party for the restoration of the caliphate. They meet in secret and number no more than a dozen.

They consider all existing states illegitimate and reject capitalism and communism alike, calling for one Islamic state under a single caliph. In Bolivia they are a curiosity, but their conspiratorial discipline resembles that of the radical student left around them on campus.

12.name: Hermanos de la Umma
12.text:
The Brothers of the Umma are a small association of Palestinian and Syrian Muslim shopkeepers in Bolivia who admire the Egyptian Muslim Brotherhood and Said Ramadan's exile network in Europe. They organize Koran lessons, charity and help for new arrivals.

The association favours Islamic ethics in public life, solidarity with the Palestinians and independence from both blocs, while respecting the laws of its host country. It avoids open politics. Its strength is a tight-knit trading community and the shops it runs in La Paz, Cochabamba and Santa Cruz.

13.name: Los Civiles de Ovando
13.text:
Ovando's Civilians are the young intellectuals and technocrats brought into the cabinet after the September 1969 coup. The most prominent is Marcelo Quiroga Santa Cruz, minister of mines and petroleum, who drafted the nationalization of the Bolivian Gulf Oil Company in October 1969.

They want the state to control oil, gas and minerals through YPFB and COMIBOL, to build smelters and to escape dependence on foreign companies, without aligning with either bloc. They have no party or mass base. Their power comes from Ovando's patronage and from public enthusiasm for the nationalization.

14.name: Partido Social Demócrata
14.text:
The Social Democratic Party is a small centrist party of La Paz professionals whose best-known figure is Luis Adolfo Siles Salinas. As vice-president he succeeded Barrientos in April 1969 and was deposed by Ovando's coup on 26 September 1969.

Despite its name, the party is moderate and conservative: it defends constitutional government, civil liberties, private property and the 1967 constitution, and seeks good relations with the United States. It opposes indefinite military rule. Its base is narrow, but Siles Salinas's brief constitutional presidency gives it moral authority among liberals and the Church.

15.name: Comité pro Santa Cruz
15.text:
The Pro Santa Cruz Civic Committee was founded in 1950 to defend the interests of the eastern lowlands against La Paz, winning in 1959 the 11 percent oil royalty for the department. It speaks for the cattle ranchers, sugar and cotton planters and merchants of the booming east.

The committee demands regional autonomy, infrastructure, credit for agribusiness and protection of private property, and it fears the miners' unions and nationalization. Anti-communist and close to the Falange, it can paralyse the city with civic strikes. Its leverage is the economic weight of Santa Cruz.

16.name: Confederación de Empresarios Privados de Bolivia
16.english: Confederation of Private Entrepreneurs of Bolivia
16.native_full: Confederación de Empresarios Privados de Bolivia
16.text:
The Confederation of Private Entrepreneurs of Bolivia was founded in 1962 to unite the chambers of commerce, industry and the medium mining companies. In 1970 it confronts a military government that has expropriated Gulf Oil and speaks of state control of the economy.

The confederation stands for free enterprise, foreign investment, legal security and restraint of the unions, and opposes the drift toward state socialism. Its members are importers, industrialists and medium mine owners in La Paz and Santa Cruz. Its leverage lies in capital, credit and connections with foreign investors.

17.name: Guardianes del Titicaca
17.text:
The Guardians of Titicaca are a circle of naturalists, university scientists and La Paz professionals inspired by Jacques Cousteau's recent expedition to Lake Titicaca, which brought world attention to its unique fauna. They study the lake, the altiplano and the eastern forests.

They call for protection of the lake, the vicuña and the Amazonian lowlands now opened to colonization and logging. Their base is tiny and academic, but their access to universities, foreign scientists and the press gives them a voice in debates on how Bolivia's resources should be used.

18.name: Movimiento Nacionalista Revolucionario
18.text:
The Revolutionary Nationalist Movement led the 1952 revolution that nationalized the tin mines, abolished the hacienda and introduced universal suffrage. Overthrown in 1964, it is split into rival factions; its founder Víctor Paz Estenssoro lives in exile in Lima, while Hernán Siles Zuazo leads another wing.

The MNR stands for national revolution: state ownership of mines, land for peasants, economic independence and a multi-class alliance under nationalist leadership. It is open to cooperation with the United States but jealous of sovereignty. Its leverage lies in its unmatched party machine, peasant syndicates and the legitimacy of 1952.

19.name: Partido Comunista Marxista-Leninista
19.text:
The Communist Party of Bolivia (Marxist-Leninist) was founded in 1965 by Óscar Zamora Medinaceli and other pro-Chinese communists who broke with the Moscow-aligned party. Zamora's broken promise of support to Che Guevara in 1967 still stains its reputation.

The party follows Peking, calling for a peasant-based people's war and denouncing both Soviet 'revisionism' and Ovando's military nationalism. It condemns the guerrilla adventurism of the ELN. Its strength lies in parts of the student movement, teachers and some miners' and peasant unions, especially in Chuquisaca and Potosí.

20.name: Pacto Militar-Campesino
20.text:
The Military-Peasant Pact was sealed in 1964 by General René Barrientos with the peasant unions of Cochabamba and the altiplano. The army pledged to protect the land reform, and the peasant leaders pledged loyalty and votes. After Barrientos's death the pact survives as the regime's rural base.

The pact offers peasants land titles, schools and roads in exchange for obedience, anti-communism and hostility to the miners' unions. It is paternalist, Catholic and patriotic. Its leverage lies in thousands of syndicate leaders who can mobilize the countryside to back or block any government in La Paz.

21.name: Unión Juvenil Cruceñista
21.text:
The Santa Cruz Youth Union was founded in 1957 as the shock force of the Pro Santa Cruz Committee during the struggle for oil royalties. Its young men fought street battles with MNR militias, and many remain close to the Bolivian Socialist Falange.

The union preaches militant regional pride, Catholic anti-communism and contempt for the highland left and the unions. It is ready to use violence, intimidation and armed action to defend Santa Cruz. Its leverage lies in its ability to control the streets of the lowland capital at short notice.

22.name: Fuerzas Armadas de la Nación
22.text:
The Armed Forces of Bolivia rule the country through the Revolutionary Government of General Alfredo Ovando Candia, who seized power on 26 September 1969. Rebuilt after 1952 with American aid, the army has been the arbiter of politics since the 1964 coup.

Under the 'Revolutionary Mandate of the Armed Forces', Ovando proclaims a nationalist revolution: Gulf Oil has been nationalized, relations with Moscow opened and union freedoms partly restored. The officer corps is divided between radicals around General Torres and conservatives around Banzer. Its power rests on arms and on its role as guardian of the state.

23.name: Leales de Charcas
23.text:
The Loyalists of Charcas gather Sucre families of old Spanish lineage who cultivate the memory of the Royal Audiencia of Charcas and admire Franco's plans to restore the Spanish crown. They meet in colonial mansions and Catholic confraternities of the constitutional capital.

They dream of a Catholic and hierarchical order under a monarch tied to the Spanish Bourbons and despise both the revolution of 1952 and the generals. They have no popular base. Their only assets are lineage, social prestige and the remnants of fortunes lost to the land reform.
